title: SLO-driven maintenance waves with KV cache warmup and safe capacity handoff
creator: Aisha Park
description:
Goal: Implement an orchestration pattern for maintenance waves that enforces per-route latency and throughput SLOs during node drains and upgrades. Key features: 1) pre-warm KV caches on standby hosts prior to traffic handoff, 2) SLO-aware drain pacing that adapts to current tail latency and throughput breach signals, 3) temporary tokenized capacity reservations to guarantee minimum throughput for critical tenants during waves, 4) graceful fallback policies to skip KV warmup or abort waves when health signals degrade.

Motivation: Current rolling upgrades and drains cause variable tail latencies and transient throughput dips for Dedicated customers. Existing drain logic is cadence-based and does not account for model KV cache cold-starts or per-route throughput contracts. By coordinating cache warmup and capacity reservations with SLO telemetry, we can reduce customer-visible regressions and allow larger, more efficient maintenance windows.

Design overview:
- Wave coordinator: new controller that computes safe batch sizes for host drains using real-time SLO metrics (p95/p99 latency, token/sec per-route).
- Warmup agents: lightweight process that replicas a subset of in-memory KV pages (prefetch heuristics based on recent prefixes) to designated warm-standby hosts. Warmup can run over NFS or use our existing cache-transfer API.
- Tokenized reservations: a short-lived lease model where critical routes reserve capacity quota from a burst pool to guarantee throughput during a wave. Leasing includes metadata for owner, duration, and fallbacks.
- Pacing policy: closed-loop controller that advances drains only when SLO headroom exists; uses exponential backoff plus bounded ramp-up when violations observed.

Trade-offs considered:
- Pre-warming increases network and memory churn; mitigations: bounded prefetch size, adaptive sampling of hot keys, and off-peak-only full warmup.
- Tokenized reservations can reduce aggregate efficiency; mitigations: aggressive reclamation and optional per-tenant caps.
- Complexity vs. reliability: we keep a simple default (conservative waves without warmup) and opt-in advanced mode for customers with throughput contracts.

Observability and telemetry: add per-wave dashboards (wave_id), events for warmup success/failure, lease acquisition/revocation, and per-route SLO deltas. Instrumentation must include KV warmup hit rate and bytes transferred.

Rollout plan:
1) Canary: implement coordinator in a non-invasive read-only mode (compute suggested wave sizes) and surface suggestions in Console (2 weeks).
2) Warmup pilot: enable warm-standby warmup for internal fleets and a single low-risk customer (3 weeks).
3) Tokenized reservations: internal tests + one enterprise customer opt-in (4 weeks).
4) Gradual ramp to default for Dedicated customers after 4 weeks of stable telemetry.

QA and testing: Synthetic load tests with realistic prefix distributions using the eval harness, chaos tests to simulate network stalls during warmup, and soak tests for reclaiming tokens. Acceptance criteria: no increase in p99 > 10% for critical routes during wave, and 90% warmup success on pilot hosts.

Rollback and failure modes: If SLO violations exceed thresholds, the coordinator aborts the wave and rebinds traffic to previous hosts. Leases are revoked and consumed tokens logged for postmortem. We will provide a manual abort action in Console.

Artifacts: design doc (Confluence) https://confluence.internal.redwood/dedicated/fleet/wave-warmup-proposal, prototype PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4128, dashboard mockups https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1WaveDashMock
